newsitem.title: USA: Germany says all troops should not leave Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Germany says all troops should not leave Bosnia.

text.p: German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said on Friday international peacekeeping troops would be needed in Bosnia again next year and that he was confident Germany would supply soldiers for such a force.

"Obviously we (NATO) have achieved a lot ... but not enough to leave Yugoslavia totally. So we have asked our authorities to study the situation," Ruehe told reporters before a meeting with U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry.

"As you know, in the past we had debates in Germany. And now we have a consensus and I'm very glad," he said in response to questions, repeating earlier predictions that NATO was likely to sponsor a new force to maintain peace in Bosnia.
"I am very confident with the decision-making process. The decision in Germany will be taken in December. That's the right time. What we are doing now is preparing," he said.

The United States has not yet committed itself to any follow-on force to replace the current NATO-led peace implementation force (IFOR) of more than 50,000 troops scheduled to leave Bosnia at the end of this year.
German units currently provide only medical and logistics support for IFOR force in a region the Nazis occupied during much of the Second World War.
But Germany last month shed some of its reluctance to send troops to Bosnia, saying in Bonn that it would be prepared to contribute infantry peacekeepers with armoured vehicles to a future mission.
Perry told Congress on Thursday President Bill Clinton was not misleading Americans on Bosnia, saying Clinton had made no decision yet on sending U.S. troops there next year.

To sharp criticism from Republicans, Perry denied that 5,000 U.S. troops who will begin entering Bosnia within days to cover the removal of 15,800 American soldiers there are the planned vanguard for a new international force in Bosnia.

But he also told the Senate Armed Services Committee that "the international interest in Bosnia has not ended," and left open the possibility that U.S. forces could be part of a possible new NATO-led peacekeeping force in 1997.

On Friday, Perry told reporters at a brief joint Pentagon news conference with Ruehe that some published reports on Thursday's hearing were incorrect in saying that the United States planned to have as many as 7,500 troops in Bosnia as late as mid-March.

He said the current plan was to have only about 7,000 U.S. troops remaining in Bosnia at the end of January and then have a rapid drawdown to about 3,000 by March 1 and none left by the middle of that month.
